about: Answer key for Computational Lab 5 (pchem_check.py). Reference values: instructor run (B3LYP/def2-SVP test set, seed 2024). Edit this plain copy in src/; the build tool encodes the students' copy.

common_mistakes.feedback: Off by a factor of 1000: the answer is asked for in meV (1 eV = 1000 meV).
Off by a factor of 27.2: a hartree ↔ eV conversion is missing, or used twice.

1.1.title: Sampling along the normal modes
1.1.setup:
_r = np.random.default_rng(1)
Xs = sample_geometry(_r, 0.6)
Qs = modes.T @ (np.sqrt(m3) * (Xs - X0).ravel())
E_harm = 0.5 * np.sum((omega * Qs)**2) / lk.ACC
E_expect = 0.6 * np.random.default_rng(1).random()

tests.hint: The geometry should hold exactly E_tot of harmonic energy. Check E_tot = E_max * rng.random() (drawn first) and Q = np.sqrt(2 * eps * lk.ACC) / omega * signs.

wrong.feedback: The geometry holds about 100 times too much energy: the amplitude needs lk.ACC, Q = np.sqrt(2 * eps * lk.ACC) / omega, because ½ω²Q² is in amu·Å²/fs², which is 1/ACC eV.
Half the energy: ε = ½ω²Q², so Q = √(2ε)/ω. The factor 2 is missing.
Twice the energy: Q = √(2ε)/ω, not 2√ε/ω or √(4ε)/ω.

1.1.ok: Each geometry carries exactly the harmonic energy you gave it, shared at random among the four modes.

1.2.title: Your test set

tests.hint: Energies relative to the minimum can't be negative: E_test = np.array([e for e, _ in ED]) - E_min.

wrong.feedback: These are total energies (about −5000 eV). Subtract the minimum: - E_min.

tests.hint: The energies should lie between 0 and about 0.6 eV, averaging about 0.3 eV. Check that you subtracted E_min (in eV).

wrong.feedback: These energies are far too large for 0.6 eV of vibrational energy. Did you subtract E_min, and are both in eV?

1.2.ok: 100 DFT points the model will never see during training: an honest test.

2.1.title: Symmetry-adapted features

tests.hint: At the linear minimum the features are (r_e, r_e, −1). cos = np.sum(b1 * b2, axis=-1) / (r1 * r2).

wrong.feedback: cos θ = +1 for the linear molecule: one bond vector points the wrong way. Both start at C: b1 = O₁ − C, b2 = O₂ − C (as given).
|cos θ| > 1: divide the dot product by the two bond lengths, / (r1 * r2).

tests.hint: For bonds of 1 and 2 Å at 90°, the features are (1, 2, 0). Use axis=-1 in the sum so it works for one geometry or many.

2.1.ok: Three numbers that don't change when the molecule moves or turns.

3.1.title: Gaussian process fit
3.1.setup:
_F = F_test[:5]
_asym = np.abs(gp.predict((_F - f_mean) / f_scale) - gp.predict((_F[:, [1, 0, 2]] - f_mean) / f_scale)).max()

tests.hint: The surface must give the same energy when the two O atoms are swapped. Add the swapped copy: Fs = np.concatenate([F, F[:, [1, 0, 2]]]) and Es = np.concatenate([E, E]).

wrong.feedback: Your surface gives different energies for (r₁, r₂) and (r₂, r₁): the O ↔ O swap isn't built in. Train on both copies, F[:, [1, 0, 2]] with the same energies E.

tests.hint: rms = np.sqrt(np.mean((E_pred - E_test)**2)) * 1000 (meV): a few hundredths of a meV.

wrong.feedback: Far too small: take the square root of the mean squared error, and convert eV → meV (× 1000).
Much larger than expected. Compare E_pred with E_test (both relative energies in eV), and check that the GP was trained with the swapped copies.

3.1.ok: Hundredths of a meV on data it never saw: as accurate as the DFT numbers themselves.

6.1.title: Harmonic frequencies of the GP surface

tests.hint: wn_gp = lk.omega_to_wavenumber(np.sqrt(np.abs(lam[5:]) * lk.ACC)): the last four eigenvalues are the vibrations.

wrong.feedback: These are the five near-zero eigenvalues (translations and rotations). The vibrations are the last four, lam[5:].
About 10× too low: ω (rad/fs) = np.sqrt(lam * lk.ACC); lk.ACC is missing.

tests.hint: The GP frequencies should agree with DFT within a few cm⁻¹.

6.1.ok: The learned surface has the right curvature: the same frequencies as DFT, from an energy fit alone.

7.1.title: Bond-charge dipole model

tests.hint: c_dip = np.linalg.lstsq(A_train, mu_train.ravel(), rcond=None)[0]: four coefficients; the first is the O charge at equilibrium, about −0.27 e.
rms_mu = np.sqrt(np.mean(np.sum((mu_pred - mu_test)**2, axis=1))): sum over x, y, z, average over geometries, then the square root.

wrong.feedback: √3 too small: sum the squared errors over x, y and z (axis=1) before averaging over the geometries.
Too small: take the square root at the end.

7.1.ok: Four numbers reproduce every test dipole to about 0.01 D.
